headline: High: B can read/write local files and run shell commands, while A is offline and file-isolated, creating a one-way data and action risk if outputs are bridged.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no filesystem read/write, stdin/stdout, clipboard, or MCP surfaces, so direct injection into A is blocked. B can read/write files and use stdin/stdout, so only an unusual manual or file bridge could carry attacker-controlled content into A. The pathway is limited and not default.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies B-generated text into A's prompt or workflow files, injection becomes possible.
IF a shared file bridge is added between A and B, B-authored content can reach A.
mitigations: Keep A and B on separate workspaces.
Disable manual copy-paste between agents during runs.
Use a read-only export format for any B output fed to A.
Add a human review step before any B output is reused.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on bridged artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A is offline and does not read files, but B can read/write the filesystem and handles configuration secrets. If A outputs are bridged into B's workspace, B can ingest them and potentially expose sensitive model assets or secrets in its outputs or API calls. The interaction is not default, but B's local-dev surface makes leakage plausible.
conditions: IF A outputs are saved into a directory that B reads, B can ingest them.
IF B is run with real secrets instead of placeholders, those secrets may be exposed through logs or outputs.
mitigations: Use separate directories for A and B.
Replace real secrets with placeholders in B.
Mount B's workspace read-only when possible.
Review B logs before sharing outputs.
requires-engineering: isolate secret-bearing services from agent outputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A cannot write files, modify git, or spawn subprocesses, so it cannot contend for mutable resources with B. B can write the filesystem and run shell commands, but without A write access or shared mutable state, the overlap is mostly read-side and low risk. Uncertainty does not justify escalation.
conditions: IF A is given filesystem write access outside its current profile, write conflicts could emerge.
IF both agents are pointed at the same mutable directory, B can overwrite A-produced artifacts.
mitigations: Keep A read-only.
Run B in a separate working directory.
Avoid shared git repositories during paired runs.
Snapshot outputs before B processes them.
requires-engineering: add locking for any shared mutable resource.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate image/workflow outputs, and B is a content-writing agent with API and stdin/stdout surfaces that may treat upstream text as input. There is no documented verification barrier between them, so if A's outputs are forwarded to B, B may propagate errors or hallucinated metadata into downstream writing. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not directly evidenced.
conditions: IF A's generated content is passed to B without verification, B may reuse it as authoritative.
IF B is tasked to summarize or publish A outputs, any A error can cascade downstream.
mitigations: Require source checks before B uses A output.
Ask B to cite provenance for any claims derived from A.
Insert a human review gate between A and B.
Limit B to formatting rather than factual transformation.
requires-engineering: add automated validation of A-to-B handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: B explicitly handles configuration secrets and requests Airflow credentials, while A is an offline image-generation tool with no secret handling. The main compliance issue is B's local-development environment and secret-bearing workflow, which can create retention or access-control mismatches if paired with A outputs in shared storage. A is not the compliance driver here, so it is cited only to show the contrast.
conditions: IF B is run with production secrets in a shared workspace, retention and access controls may be violated.
IF A outputs are stored alongside B's secret-bearing artifacts, compliance boundaries blur.
mitigations: Use non-production secrets in B.
Store A outputs separately from B artifacts.
Rotate any exposed credentials after the run.
Review retention settings for B logs.
requires-engineering: enforce secret segregation and retention policy controls.
